title: The Computer That Would Think: Japan's Fifth Generation Project, 1982–1992
search_title: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer project 1982–1992: the plan, the panic, the result
description: In 1982, Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry launched a ten-year national programme to build a computer that could reason, converse in natural language, and leapfrog Western computing entirely. The announcement set off a global alarm, triggering rival programmes in the United States, Britain, and Europe. This essay traces the plan's origins in the mind of a mid-level bureaucrat, the genuine technical achievements of ICOT, and why a project that met most of its own goals came to be remembered as a failure.
standfirst: In October 1981, Japan told the world it was going to build a computer that thinks. What happened next was less a technology race than a mirror in which every participant saw a different threat.
body:
## Tokyo, October 1981 Back in their respective capitals, they did not cooperate. They panicked. Invitations had arrived unsolicited at computer science departments around the world. Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry had convened an international conference in Tokyo to present a plan for the next generation of computing. Around eighty researchers from fourteen countries attended; around three hundred people came in total, including invited speaker Edward Feigenbaum of Stanford University, the American expert-systems pioneer.1 Moto-oka's opening keynote stated Japan's intention to be a full partner in the international scientific community and called for future cooperation; Feigenbaum concluded his own talk with the same appeal.2 ## The Dream The idea had begun not in a government ministry but over a few heady afternoons in 1978, in the office of a mid-level MITI manager named Masataka Nakano. As the cultural critic Jun'ichiro Uemae describes in his retrospective *Japanizu Dorimu*, Nakano was then only thirty, running a handful of young programmers as a division chief on the fourth-generation VLSI project.3 Nakano's concern was not primarily about computing power. He was not a programmer and had no technical background; he was therefore, as the historian Colin Garvey notes in his account of the project, keenly aware of the social cost of computerisation in the Japanese office.4 Computers of the late 1970s were enormous machines requiring specialised training. Most government officials at MITI could not use them. Computer interfaces, where they were not purely numerical, were in English: Japanese users had to acquire a non-trivial amount of English on top of the technical knowledge itself, a considerable barrier. The result was that rather than streamlining the Japanese office, computers were adding to its burden. There was a geopolitical dimension as well. IBM dominated the international computer market through users' need for backward compatibility. Even competitors who built technically superior machines found that potential customers replied that if the machines could not run existing IBM software, they could not use them.5 Nakano saw this as locking Japan into an endless cycle of imitation. He resolved to break it, telling his team: "This is why Japan has to be first to build a non-von Neumann machine. If we do, then we can race down an original path, outside of the world controlled by IBM."6 This was the seed of the Fifth Generation. Its name followed the accepted lineage of computing hardware: vacuum tubes (first generation), transistors (second), integrated circuits (third), very large-scale integrated circuits (fourth).7 The fifth would be something categorically different: machines that operated not on sequential numerical instructions but on logical inference, in parallel, accepting natural-language input from ordinary users. Nakano himself was rotated to a new post in another MITI division in 1979, just as the formal planning committee formed. Two-year rotations were, as Uemae notes, an entirely ordinary feature of Japanese working life. His name consequently does not appear in the official FGCS literature.8 The planning committee that emerged from his idea was chaired by Moto-oka and included three subcommittees, on Basic Theory, Computer Architecture, and Social Impacts, led respectively by Kazuhiro Fuchi, Hideo Aiso, and Hajime Karatsu.9 Around one hundred representatives from science, industry, and government participated in as many meetings over two years. The committee's ambitions were social as much as technical. As Karatsu's Social Impacts subcommittee set out in its preliminary report, the Fifth Generation computer would increase productivity in low-productivity areas, meet international competition by augmenting rather than replacing Japan's skilled labour force, assist in saving energy and resources, and help cope with an ageing society.10 Chairman Moto-oka later described this aspiration to Western readers in the title of his 1983 *IEEE Spectrum* article: "A Quantum Jump in Friendliness", a computer that fits the needs of people instead of making people work by the rules of the machine.11 What the committee explicitly did not call it was an artificial intelligence project. The Japanese term *jinkō chinō*, artificial intelligence, was American in origin and American in flavour. What ICOT would pursue was *chishiki jōhō shori shisutemu*: knowledge information processing systems. The distinction mattered to the planners. As Fuchi later asserted, responding to those who conflated the Fifth Generation with American AI: "our project is not an artificial intelligence project or an expert system project as wrongly understood by some people."12 ## The Wager In April 1982, MITI formally launched the project, establishing ICOT as a joint venture between the ministry and eight of Japan's largest computer and electronics manufacturers: Fujitsu, Hitachi, NEC, Toshiba, Mitsubishi Electric, Matsushita, Oki Electric, and Sharp.13 By 1982, Japan already held 74 percent of its own domestic computer market, making it, as the political economist Marie Anchordoguy found, "the only industrialized country in the free world where IBM was not the market leader."14 The institute opened in Tokyo under the direction of Kazuhiro Fuchi, who came from MITI's own Electrotechnical Laboratory. To the laboratory came forty young engineers and scientists, most in their twenties, from those eight firms.15 The project was to run for ten years in three phases: an initial stage focused on basic research (1982–1985), an intermediate stage on subsystems (1985–1989), and a final stage on complete prototype systems (1989–1992). MITI had initially stipulated that the funds it planned to spend over the decade would be matched by the eight participating firms, for a total of nearly $1 billion at then-prevailing exchange rates; because industry never agreed to match, MITI spent approximately ¥54 billion alone over the eleven fiscal years of the programme's operation, confirmed by the Information Processing Society of Japan's Computer Museum.16 The technical wager at the heart of the project rested on two linked bets. The first was that the correct language for the fifth generation kernel was Prolog, rather than Lisp, the American AI community's standard tool. Prolog was a logic programming language developed in Europe: invented in Marseille in 1972 by Alain Colmerauer and his team, with key theoretical contributions from Robert Kowalski in Edinburgh, whose procedural interpretation of Horn clauses provided Prolog's logical foundation.17 Fuchi had been impressed by logic programming on visits abroad and saw it as the "missing link" between knowledge information processing and the non-von Neumann hardware he intended to build. His choice of Prolog drew the ire of the American AI community: one influential commentator remarked that "Prolog is seen as somehow 'un-American' — a European fad that has now been taken up by the Japanese..."18 Fuchi defended the choice by arguing that Prolog was technically superior and that Japan, as a newcomer, had no obligation to adopt the legacy language Lisp.19 The second bet was on massive parallelism. Performance targets were set in a project-specific unit, LIPS, Logical Inferences Per Second. Where a typical workstation of the early 1980s ran Prolog at roughly 100,000 LIPS, the project aimed for 100 million to 1 billion LIPS: three to four orders of magnitude of improvement, to be achieved by designing special-purpose parallel hardware from scratch.20 The industry participants were not enthusiastic. When they learned that Fuchi's plan had been approved and that the Fifth Generation computers would not be IBM-compatible, the eight firms attempted to back out of the project entirely.21 MITI applied pressure by threatening exclusion from future government funding opportunities, and industry eventually relented, though the companies never agreed to match funds as MITI had initially stipulated. Instead, they conceded to sending researchers on a rotating basis to ICOT.22 Fuchi accepted the directorship of ICOT on two conditions, both radical within Japanese business culture: that he could choose any computer manufacturer to provide terminals during the initial phase, including American machines, and that researchers seconded to ICOT were to be under thirty-five years old.23 He then signalled his intention to run the institute as an autonomous research institution free from commercial pressure, by regularly and painstakingly emphasising that the project had "no commercial objectives."24 Results were to be shared openly: published in scientific articles and conference presentations, in English as well as Japanese. ICOT would be a global research hub. As Fuchi put it, the project "must not be exclusive or closed to outsiders."25 ## The Panic The Western response to the 1981 Tokyo conference was immediate and, in the United States particularly, alarmed. The announcement came, as Feigenbaum and Howard Shrobe observed in a survey of the project written around 1987–88, "on the heels of MITI's highly successful efforts to promote Japanese prowess in consumer electronics and computer chips," and it "set off alarm bells in capitals and companies of the West."26 Britain moved first. A UK Department of Industry mission had attended the Tokyo conference, and its participants returned with a new assessment: rather than collaboration with the Japanese, there was "an urgent need for the U.K. to form its own fifth-generation computing strategy."27 The British government convened a committee under John Alvey of British Telecom, which produced a report proposing a collaborative government-industry research programme. The result was the Alvey Programme, launched in 1983, which the *Financial Times* announced under the headline "Britain Enters the Great Race."28 The United States followed a different logic. Feigenbaum returned home and began travelling the country giving seminars to computer scientists and government officials. His argument took book form in 1983 as *The Fifth Generation: Artificial Intelligence and Japan's Computer Challenge to the World*, co-authored with Pamela McCorduck and published by Addison-Wesley.29 The authors were frank that they were "decidedly not disinterested observers," and the book's conclusion called on Americans to mount a large-scale national project because failure to respond would mean consigning "our nation to the role of the first great postindustrial agrarian society."30 The book proved highly successful and widely influential, and was even a bestseller in Japan.31 Feigenbaum then testified before Congress in June 1983. He warned that the era of "reasoning machines is inevitable. It is the 'manifest destiny' of computing," and offered three options: a coordinated national response, an ICOT-like centre, or nothing and disaster.32 Congress embraced the alarm. Two major American programmes followed. The Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation, a for-profit industrial consortium of thirteen corporations, was founded in September 1983. DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative, a decade-long, $1 billion applications-oriented project to create autonomous weapons and AI systems for each branch of the military, was signed by President Reagan in December 1983.33 There is a detail worth dwelling on. Robert Cooper, the DARPA director, and Robert Kahn, director of DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office, had both attended the 1981 Tokyo conference. They returned, according to the historians Alex Roland and Philip Shiman, with a quite different impression: the Japanese were still trailing the United States in computing and were headed down a dead-end. This analysis did not stop them from exploiting Feigenbaum's alarmism. In later interviews, Cooper confessed to trundling out the Japanese "as the arch-enemies" and using the alarm "unabashedly" in private conversations with members of Congress.34 Europe joined the race with the European Strategic Programme on Research in Information Technology, ESPRIT, funded at nearly $2 billion over five years.35 And then there was the Soviet Union. Western actors hardly noticed when the USSR, the last of the major powers to enter the race, launched its own response. The five-year Soviet plan coordinated computing projects across Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, and the Soviet Union and was funded at a comparatively modest $100 million for 1984 to 1989.36 Feigenbaum and McCorduck's book, the document most responsible for generating the alarm, had dismissed the Soviets in less than two pages as doing "pretty boring stuff."37 That even Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, and the USSR felt compelled to respond says something about the scale of the panic; that the West barely noticed the response says something about who the panic was really for. Where ICOT was organised around shared research with published results and no commercial objectives, the American Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation almost immediately "shrouded much of its research in secrecy to protect shareholder advantage," resulting, as *IEEE Spectrum* reported, in forced "isolation between projects" that undermined the potential benefits of cooperation.38 The Strategic Computing Initiative was explicitly military in aim. The Alvey Programme was decentralised across universities and firms rather than concentrated in a single institute. All of them, in their different ways, replaced ICOT's model of open, disinterested research for the public good with the logic of the market or the military. ## What Was Actually Built Phase One of ICOT's work ran from 1982 to March 1985 and focused on logic programming. An early model of logic processing hardware was designed by ICOT and manufactured by Mitsubishi: a minicomputer workstation called PSI, the Personal Sequential Inference machine. A faster version, PSI-2, followed; a high-speed version called CHI was built by NEC for ICOT.39 ICOT then extended and reworked Prolog into a powerful programming tool in which the operating software of their machines could be written. This effort, done under contract by Mitsubishi, resulted in the largest Prolog program by far ever written.40 However, when the project moved into Phase Two and the challenge became combining logic programming with massive parallelism, a language shift occurred. During a visit to ICOT, Ehud Shapiro, a logician who would later co-author the 1993 retrospective assessment of the project, developed what the *Fifty Years of Prolog* survey defines as a subset of concurrent Prolog that left out backtracking to reduce the implementation complexity.41 Shapiro's work inspired Kazuhiro Ueda's Guarded Horn Clauses language (GHC), and from GHC came a new kernel language called KL1 (Kernel Language 1, a concurrent logic language), which became the core language of the entire project from Phase Two onward.42 The same survey notes that with this departure from Prolog, "an essential part of the language's elegance and functionality was lost, and this arguably detracted from the potential impact of the FGCS."43 The man whose visit had set the shift in motion was later among those who said so most plainly. Phase Two produced the Parallel Inference Machine, or PIM: clusters of PSI machines running logic programs in parallel. Phase Three, the final stage, produced five architecturally distinct PIM models, used to run and evaluate demonstration software in domains including molecular biology, legal reasoning, and logic circuit design.44 ICOT also developed PIMOS (the operating system for the parallel inference machines, written in KL1) and KLIC (a compiler that translates KL1 into standard C, freeing programs from dependence on special-purpose hardware). The Information Processing Society of Japan's Computer Museum records that the project produced the world's fastest and largest computer oriented toward knowledge information processing, with two PIM models now preserved at the National Museum of Nature and Science in Tokyo.45 ## Why It Failed, and Why the Verdict Is Harder to Read Most technical goals were met. Almost no industrial legacy survived. The word "failure" attached itself to the Fifth Generation so quickly and thoroughly that it is now difficult to assess the project without first noticing that the verdict was partly imported from outside. As Ehud Shapiro and David Warren, two researchers who worked on the project, observed in their 1993 retrospective, the West had perceived Japan as "promising to make the dream of artificial intelligence (AI) come true", claims that were "further amplified by scientists around the world, who capitalized on the fear of Japanese technological supremacy in order to scare their own governments into funding research."46 When Japanese computers had not dominated the global economy by the early 1990s, many in the West judged the project a failure by the standard of goals that the project itself had never set. Fuchi noted the resulting Catch-22 with some bitterness. Noting how "an exaggerated image of the project was engendered" early and seemed to persist, he complained that the project first had to face criticism, based on that false image, "that it was a reckless project trying to tackle impossible goals", and then faced the criticism "that the project has failed because it has been unable to realize those grand goals."47 The most sustained contemporary scholarly dissent came from J. Marshall Unger, whose 1987 book *The Fifth Generation Fallacy* argued that the West had completely misunderstood Japan's interest in AI.48 Unger's central claim was that the project had been motivated above all by Japan's need to overcome the problems of its own writing system for computing, a domestic, linguistic problem, not a bid for global economic dominance. This affirmative thesis was received sceptically by the scholarly community: the 1988 *Computational Linguistics* review found Unger's writing-system argument "quite preposterous," though its final verdict was the Scottish one: not proven.49 But Unger's diagnosis of Western mischaracterisation, his attack on the Feigenbaum-McCorduck account of the project as an economic threat, was well taken, and the book is a reminder that the FGCS was consistently misread on both sides of the alarm. There was, however, a genuine technical problem, and it was not Japan's alone. The core bet of the Fifth Generation, that inference grounded in symbolic logic was the road to machine intelligence, was the mainstream view in AI research worldwide in the 1980s. Over the same decade, general-purpose processors improved in performance and fell in price at a pace that nobody anticipated. By the time the PIM hardware was complete, RISC workstations and Intel-based PCs had overtaken purpose-built inference machines on price-performance, bringing the collapse of expert-systems investment across the field that became known as the second AI winter.50 The gap between ICOT's research and commercial practice was visible long before the project ended. Feigenbaum and Shrobe, writing in the late 1980s, found that even ICOT's own member companies were "making little or no direct use of the ICOT research results." Fujitsu, the commercial AI leader in Japan, sold a Lisp machine derivative of American designs rather than a Prolog machine; its best-selling expert-systems shell was Lisp-based and derived from Stanford University software.51 The problem was not merely that the project left no commercial bridge at its close; the bridge was never being built during the project itself. This was not a uniquely Japanese miscalculation. DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative "did not quite end; it simply disappeared," having "vanished" from the DARPA budget by 1993, in Roland and Shiman's account.52 The American market for special-purpose AI hardware collapsed in 1987. The Alvey Programme concluded with mixed results. What Daniel Crevier, in his history of AI, called the "Rollercoaster of the 1980s" resulted in near-total collapse by the end of the decade across all the major programmes.53 There was also what the post-project assessments identified as a specifically Japanese institutional problem. ICOT had no permanent research staff: it was composed entirely of secondees from companies, turning over en masse at each stage boundary. Institutional memory was very difficult to accumulate. When the project concluded in 1992, no permanent entity existed anywhere with responsibility for bridging the results into commercial products.54 On the other hand, the staffing model did produce a training effect that ICOT itself always regarded as its first and most important achievement. By the end of Phase One in 1985, ICOT managers counted approximately 1,000 trained engineers in the field, including ICOT researchers, engineers in the cooperating sections of member company laboratories, and engineers in the proprietary sections.55 The project concluded in 1992, with a final international conference in 1993. ICOT then released its software deliverables free of charge as ICOT Free Software, including the PIMOS source code and KLIC, made available on the young internet, allowing researchers worldwide to continue building on the project's language work without needing access to the PIM hardware.56 Compared to its Western counterparts, the verdict on the Fifth Generation is paradoxical. The SCI, MCC, Alvey, and ESPRIT are typically remembered as partial successes; Japan's project is remembered as an outright failure. Daniel Crevier's framing is representative: whereas the SCI merely "disappointed its military sponsors," the Japanese, he claims, "fell far short of their objectives."57 ICOT met most of its own technical milestones. The SCI vanished from its budget. Alvey concluded years before the Fifth Generation finished. The American market for AI hardware collapsed two years before ICOT's final conference. On any neutral accounting, the programmes had roughly comparable records of technical achievement and commercial non-delivery. What the Fifth Generation did not deliver was the one thing it had explicitly not promised: commercial dominance of the global computing market. That goal was Feigenbaum's, not Fuchi's. MITI considered the project a success on its own merits, a view confirmed by Nakamura and Shibuya's 1996 analysis of Japanese technology policy.58 Economic payoff, as Feigenbaum and Shrobe conceded in their own 1993 evaluation of the project, was never among ICOT's stated goals.59 The deeper failure was one of the bet itself, shared with the entire field. Nobody in 1982, not Fuchi, not Moto-oka, not the DARPA planners, not the Alvey committee, foresaw that the mid-1990s would bring a personal computing revolution built on exactly the von Neumann architecture that the Fifth Generation had proposed to replace. As the leading University of Tokyo AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo later reflected: "I know there is no 'What if?' in history, but my dream is to imagine that if the Web had appeared 15 years earlier, Japan would be sitting where Silicon Valley is right now."60 The supposed failure left a long shadow in Japan. From roughly 1997 to 2002, Matsuo observed, AI was so taboo in Japanese computing circles that to use even the Japanese word for it, *jinkō chinō*, drew condemnation.61 ## What Remains The Fifth Generation project was the first national, large-scale AI research and development programme to be conducted without military funding or explicit commercial objectives, a fact that Garvey describes as comparatively unique among the national computing projects of the era.62 Its results were published openly, in English as well as Japanese, and eventually released on the young internet. Hundreds of international researchers visited ICOT each year. It built genuine hardware, five PIM models, two of which are in a national museum, and contributed significantly to the field of concurrent logic programming. It was also, by any reasonable measure, a bet on the wrong approach, made at a moment when the whole field was betting the same way. The difference was that MITI's version of the bet was more visible, more explicitly national in its ambitions, and more thoroughly presented as a threat by people who had their own reasons to raise the alarm. When the bet failed, alongside all the Western bets made in response, only Japan was called the loser. Nakano, the civil servant who had the idea in 1978 and was then rotated out of the project before it began, was on a business trip in New York when the Tokyo conference of 1981 set the world computing community in motion.63 By the time the project closed, Fuchi and his colleagues had spent a decade being told they were building either a monster or a failure, depending on the year and the continent. The monster never appeared. The failure is harder to locate than the histories suggest. The ICOT Free Software release, a publicly funded research archive placed on the open internet at no charge, remains, on the record, a better model for what publicly funded AI research can look like than anything the alarm produced on the other side of the Pacific.64
